questions.q: This lesson frames privilege escalation findings primarily as what?
options: Clever, novel tricks unique to a skilled tester
Misconfiguration findings a hardening audit is already designed to catch
Random chance discoveries that can't be systematically searched for
Findings that only matter if a live attacker happens to find them first
questions.explain: Every category in this lesson is a documented misconfiguration class that a routine hardening/CIS Benchmark review already checks for, independent of active testing.

questions.q: What makes an unquoted Windows service path a finding?
options: It causes the service to crash on every reboot
It slows down service startup time measurably
Windows may try an ambiguous shorter path first, which can run an attacker-placed file in a writable location
It only matters on services that run as a low-privilege account
questions.explain: An unquoted path with spaces creates ambiguity in how Windows parses it, and an audit checks whether that ambiguous shorter path is writable by a low-privilege account.

questions.q: A sudoers entry with NOPASSWD on a broad or file-manipulating command is risky because:
options: It effectively grants root-level access without a password prompt
It only affects commands that are already deprecated
It slows down the sudo command's performance
NOPASSWD entries are automatically disabled after 24 hours
questions.explain: A NOPASSWD entry on a command broad enough to read or write arbitrary files effectively hands over root access without any further authentication step.

questions.q: Why does an audit flag a custom binary with the SUID bit set, owned by root?
options: It means the file was downloaded from an untrusted source
SUID has no real security implication and is flagged only by convention
The binary runs with root's privileges rather than the caller's, which is dangerous if the binary isn't a trusted system tool
SUID binaries are always malware
questions.explain: SUID makes a binary execute with its owner's privileges; an unusual binary with root ownership and the SUID bit set is exactly the pattern a hardening scan looks for.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect privilege-escalation findings back to course 8's hardening content?
options: It says the two topics are unrelated and shouldn't be compared
Hardening courses only cover topics that pentesting never touches
Privilege escalation techniques are newly discovered each time, with no overlap to prior hardening material
A pentest's escalation phase proves an already-known, already-documented risk category exists unremediated on a specific host
questions.explain: The categories in this lesson are the same ones course 8's hardening/CIS Benchmark content already teaches defenders to check for — a pentest proves the unremediated instance, it doesn't invent a new risk category.
